questions.q: Which mineral is mainly used in making steel, about 10 kg of it being needed to make one tonne of steel?
questions.e: Manganese is also used to make bleaching powder, insecticides and paints.

questions.q: In Jowai and Cherrapunjee in Meghalaya, coal is dug out by family members through long narrow tunnels. This is called ______ mining.
questions.e: In Meghalaya, mineral ownership lies with individuals and communities, and rat-hole mining is done by family members.

questions.q: Which range of hills in the Bastar district of Chhattisgarh produces very high-grade haematite iron ore?
questions.e: Bailadila ore is exported to Japan and South Korea via Visakhapatnam port.

questions.q: The Khetri mines in Rajasthan are famous for which mineral?
questions.e: The Balaghat mines in Madhya Pradesh and the Khetri mines in Rajasthan are important for copper.

questions.q: India has experimental geothermal energy projects in the Parvati valley near Manikarn in Himachal Pradesh and in the ______ valley in Ladakh.
questions.e: Geothermal energy is heat and electricity produced using heat from the interior of the earth.

questions.q: In which year did Sri Lanka emerge as an independent country?
questions.e: After independence in 1948, leaders of the Sinhala community sought to secure dominance over government by virtue of their majority.

questions.q: In 1956, an Act was passed in Sri Lanka to recognise which as its only official language?
questions.e: The Act disregarded Tamil and was one of the majoritarian measures that alienated Sri Lankan Tamils.

questions.q: Which city was chosen as the headquarters of the European Union?
questions.e: Belgium's arrangement for sharing power in Brussels made the city suitable as the headquarters of the EU.

questions.q: Sharing of power among governments at different levels, such as the union, state and local governments, is called ______ division of power.
questions.e: In vertical division, higher and lower levels of government share power.

questions.q: In horizontal power sharing, each organ of government checks the others. This arrangement is called a system of checks and ______.
questions.e: Checks and balances ensure that none of the organs can exercise unlimited power.

questions.q: Between 1970 and 1993, how many times did Belgium amend its constitution to accommodate its language communities?
questions.e: The Belgian leaders amended their constitution four times to work out an arrangement in which everyone could live together.

questions.q: According to the Sri Lankan constitution, the state shall protect and foster which religion?
questions.e: This provision was one of the measures that made Sri Lankan Tamils feel that the constitution denied them equal rights.

questions.q: When two or more political parties come together to form a government, it is called a ______ government.
questions.e: A coalition government is a form of power sharing among political parties.

questions.q: According to NCERT, Sinhala speakers form about what percentage of Sri Lanka's population?
questions.e: Sinhala speakers form about 74 per cent and Tamil speakers about 18 per cent of the population.

questions.q: Tamils in Sri Lanka whose forefathers came from India as plantation workers during the colonial period are called ______ Tamils.
questions.e: Of the 18 per cent Tamil speakers, 13 per cent are Sri Lankan Tamils and the rest are Indian Tamils.

questions.q: Which kind of reason for power sharing holds that it is the very spirit of democracy, and not merely a way of avoiding conflict?
questions.e: Prudential reasons stress better outcomes, while moral reasons treat power sharing as valuable in itself.

questions.q: The Belgian constitution prescribes that the number of Dutch-speaking and French-speaking ministers in the central government shall be ______.
questions.e: Some special laws require the support of the majority of members from each linguistic group, so no single community can make decisions unilaterally.

questions.q: Subjects of national importance such as defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications and currency are included in the ______ List.
questions.e: The Union government alone can make laws on the subjects in the Union List.

questions.q: Subjects of state and local importance such as police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation are included in the ______ List.
questions.e: The state governments alone can make laws on the subjects in the State List.

questions.q: The president of a gram panchayat is called the ______.
questions.e: The gram panchayat is a council of ward members (panch) and a president (sarpanch).

questions.q: Federations like the USA, Switzerland and Australia, formed when independent states come together to form a bigger unit, are called ______ federations.
questions.e: In coming-together federations, all the constituent states usually have equal power and are strong vis-a-vis the federal government.

questions.q: In a municipal corporation, the political head is called the ______.
questions.e: The municipal chairperson is the political head of a municipality; in a municipal corporation the officer is called the mayor.

questions.q: All the panchayat samitis or mandals in a district together constitute the ______.
questions.e: Most members of the zilla parishad are elected; MPs and MLAs of the district and some officials are also members.

questions.q: Which independent institution has been created in each state to conduct panchayat and municipal elections?
questions.e: The 1992 amendment provided for a State Election Commission in each state.

questions.q: All the voters in a village are members of the ______, which supervises the work of the gram panchayat and must meet at least twice or thrice a year.
questions.e: The gram sabha approves the annual budget of the gram panchayat and reviews its performance.

questions.q: How many languages are included in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution as Scheduled Languages?
questions.e: Besides Hindi, 21 other languages are recognised as Scheduled Languages.

questions.q: In which year did Belgium shift from a unitary to a federal form of government?
questions.e: In 1993 the regional governments of Belgium were given constitutional powers that were no longer dependent on the central government.

questions.q: Areas like Chandigarh and Lakshadweep, which are too small to become independent states and could not be merged with existing ones, are called ______.
questions.e: Union Territories do not have the powers of a state; the central government has special powers in running them.

questions.q: The fundamental provisions of India's federal structure cannot be changed by the Union government alone.
p: (a) With what majority must a change be passed in both Houses of Parliament?
Two-thirds|Two thirds|2/3|Two-third
(b) At least what fraction of the total states must then ratify the change through their legislatures?
Half|One-half|One half|1/2
(c) Which institution acts as an umpire if disputes arise between different levels of government?
Supreme Court|Courts|Judiciary|Highest court
questions.e: An amendment needs a two-thirds majority in both Houses and ratification by at least half of the states; the courts settle disputes over the division of powers.

questions.q: A political party has three components: the leaders, the active members and the ______.
questions.e: Followers support the party; active members and leaders run it.

questions.q: A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government is called a ______.
questions.e: Political parties agree on some policies and programmes for society with a view to promoting the collective good.

questions.q: Which political party was founded in 1885?
questions.e: The Indian National Congress, one of the oldest parties in the world, played a dominant role in Indian politics after independence.

questions.q: The Bahujan Samaj Party was formed in 1984 under the leadership of ______.
questions.e: The BSP seeks to represent and secure power for the bahujan samaj, which includes Dalits, Adivasis, OBCs and religious minorities.

questions.q: In which year was the Bharatiya Janata Party founded?
questions.e: The BJP was founded in 1980 by reviving the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, formed in 1951 by Syama Prasad Mukherjee.

questions.q: When several parties in a multiparty system join hands to contest elections and win power, the grouping is called an alliance or a ______.
questions.e: Examples given by NCERT include the NDA, the UPA and the Left Front.

questions.q: A party that secures at least six per cent of the votes in a State Legislative Assembly election and wins at least two seats is recognised as a ______ party.
questions.e: The Election Commission lays down these criteria; state parties are commonly called regional parties.

questions.q: In which year was the Communist Party of India (Marxist) founded?
questions.e: The CPI(M) was founded in 1964; the Communist Party of India dates from 1925.

questions.q: The Supreme Court has made it mandatory for every candidate who contests elections to file an ______ giving details of property and criminal cases.
questions.e: This information is made public so that voters can make an informed choice.

questions.q: A person who is strongly committed to a party, group or faction is called a ______.
questions.e: Partisanship is marked by a tendency to take a side and an inability to take a balanced view.

questions.q: The Election Commission has made it necessary for political parties to hold organisational elections and file their ______ returns.
questions.e: This is one of the steps taken to reform political parties.

questions.q: When top positions in a party are always controlled by members of one family, the challenge is called ______ succession.
questions.e: Dynastic succession is unfair to other members and bad for democracy, since people without adequate experience may reach positions of power.

questions.q: The number of children who die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1000 live children born in that year is called the ______.
questions.e: The infant mortality rate is an important indicator of health facilities.

questions.q: The proportion of the literate population in the 7 years and above age group is called the ______.
questions.e: The literacy rate is one of the indicators used to compare levels of education.

questions.q: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the needs of future generations is called ______ development.
questions.e: Sustainability of development is essential because many resources, like groundwater and crude oil, can be exhausted.

questions.q: The total number of children of age group 14 and 15 years attending school as a percentage of the total number of children of the same age group is called the ______.
questions.e: The net attendance ratio is used to compare how many children in an age group actually attend school.

questions.q: Which index, calculated by dividing a person's weight in kg by the square of the height in metres, is used to find out whether adults are undernourished?
questions.e: A BMI below 18.5 indicates that a person is undernourished; above 25 indicates overweight.

questions.q: Which international organisation uses per capita income in its World Development Report to classify countries?
questions.e: The World Development Report classifies countries as rich or low-income on the basis of per capita income.

questions.q: Equal treatment, freedom, security and respect for others are ______ goals of development.
questions.e: People seek not only more income but also things that cannot be easily measured in money.

questions.q: The average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth is called ______.
questions.e: Life expectancy at birth is one of the indicators in the Human Development Report.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-material goal of development?
questions.e: Equal treatment cannot be bought with money; the others are material goals.

questions.q: Besides life expectancy and education, which indicator does the Human Development Index use?
questions.a: Per capita income|Income|Gross national income per capita|GNI per capita
questions.e: The HDI combines health, education and per capita income to compare countries.

questions.q: In the Human Development Report, the average number of years of education received by people aged 25 and above is called mean years of ______.
questions.e: Mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling are the education indicators in the report.

questions.q: Things like security, pollution-free environment and protection from infectious diseases are cheaper to provide collectively. Such facilities are called ______ facilities.
questions.e: Money in hand cannot buy all the goods and services needed to live well; some are best provided collectively.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Activities that produce goods by exploiting natural resources, such as agriculture, dairy, fishing and forestry, belong to the ______ sector.
questions.e: The primary sector is also called the agriculture and related sector.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: The sector in which natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing is the ______ sector.
questions.e: The secondary sector is also called the industrial sector, since it is associated with different kinds of industries.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Activities that do not produce a good themselves but aid production, such as transport, banking and trade, belong to the tertiary or ______ sector.
questions.e: The tertiary sector generates services rather than goods.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: The value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year is called its ______.
questions.e: GDP shows how big the economy is; in India it is measured by a central government ministry.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: A situation in which people are working less than their potential, for example when more people than needed work on a family farm, is called ______.
questions.e: In such a case each worker is working, but no one is fully employed.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Small and scattered units, largely outside the control of the government, where jobs are low-paid and often not regular, form the ______ sector.
questions.e: Unorganised sector workers have no provision for overtime, paid leave or holidays, and can be asked to leave without reason.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Tata Iron and Steel Company Limited and Reliance Industries Limited are owned by private individuals. They are in the ______ sector.
questions.e: Activities in the private sector are guided by the motive to earn profits.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Under MGNREGA, if the government fails in its duty to provide employment, it must give ______ to the people.
questions.e: MGNREGA makes the right to work a legal entitlement for rural households.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: According to NCERT, which sector continues to be the largest employer in India, with more than half of the workers?
questions.e: Although the tertiary sector produces the largest share of GDP, most workers are still in the primary sector, mainly agriculture.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Organised sector workers get paid leave, payment during holidays, gratuity and a ______ fund, to which the employer also contributes.
questions.e: These benefits make jobs in the organised sector more secure than those in the unorganised sector.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Only the value of final goods and services is counted in GDP. This is done to avoid ______ counting.
questions.e: The value of final goods already includes the value of all the intermediate goods used in making them.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: A farmer sells wheat to a flour mill for ₹8 per kg. The mill grinds it and sells the flour to a biscuit company for ₹10 per kg. Using the flour and other things, the company makes four packets of biscuits and sells them to consumers for ₹60.
p: (a) Which of these is the final good?
Biscuits|Biscuit
(b) What value should be counted in GDP for this chain of production?
(c) How much value does the flour mill add per kg?
questions.e: Only the final good, biscuits worth ₹60, is counted; the mill adds ₹10 - ₹8 = ₹2 per kg.

questions.q: The exchange of goods for goods without the use of money is called the ______ system.
questions.e: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants, which money eliminates.

questions.q: A paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from a person's account to the person in whose name it has been issued is called a ______.
questions.e: Cheques allow payments to be made directly from demand deposits without cash.

questions.q: In a barter system, both parties must want to sell what the other wishes to buy. This is called a double ______ of wants.
questions.e: Money acts as a medium of exchange and removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.

questions.q: Which institution issues currency notes on behalf of the central government in India?
questions.e: According to Indian law, no other individual or organisation is allowed to issue currency.

questions.q: The rupee is widely accepted as a medium of exchange because the law legalises its use. It is therefore called legal ______.
questions.e: No individual in India can legally refuse a payment made in rupees.

questions.q: Interest rate, collateral, documentation requirement and mode of repayment together make up the ______ of credit.
questions.e: Terms of credit vary depending on the nature of the lender and the borrower.

questions.q: According to NCERT, banks in India these days hold about what percentage of their deposits as cash?
questions.e: Banks keep about 15 per cent as cash to pay depositors who may come to withdraw, and use most of the rest to extend loans.

questions.q: Loans from banks and cooperatives are called ______ sector loans.
questions.e: Moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends make up the informal sector.

questions.q: Self-Help Groups aim to organise the rural poor, in particular ______, into small groups that pool their savings.
questions.e: A typical SHG has 15 to 20 members, usually belonging to one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly.

questions.q: After a year or two of regular savings, a Self-Help Group becomes eligible to take a loan from a ______.
questions.e: The loan is sanctioned in the name of the group and is meant to create self-employment opportunities for members.

questions.q: A farmer needs ₹10,000 for 6 months. A moneylender charges simple interest of 3% per month, while a bank charges simple interest of 12% per year.
p: (a) What is the moneylender's interest for one month?
(b) What is the moneylender's total interest for 6 months?
(c) What is the bank's interest for 6 months?
(d) Which of the two is a formal source of credit?
Bank|The bank
questions.e: 3% of ₹10,000 is ₹300 a month, or ₹1,800 for 6 months; at 12% a year the bank charges ₹600 for half a year. Banks are formal lenders.
